title: Histogram with competing distribution models
what_it_asks: You are given a histogram of a data set, and usually a normal model and a curve model defined by a function. You estimate frequencies or probabilities from the histogram using area, then compare them with what each model predicts. The idea is that area represents frequency, and for a continuous model probability is area under the curve, found by integration or a calculator.
typical_structure: Questions usually have about four parts, though they range from one part to seven, and every one has a diagram. Most parts carry 2 or 3 marks, with the odd 1-mark statement. Early parts read the histogram: find a frequency, a mean, a quartile or an estimated probability. Middle parts often say "show that" or "hence" and use integration of the fitted curve. A last part usually asks you to comment on which model fits better, with a reason.
mark_pattern: The most typical part is a 2-mark M1 A1: a method line, then the correct value. Single B1 marks are also typical, for a stated value, a read-off or a comment. Three-mark parts may run B1 B1 dB1 (two correct statements, then a dependent conclusion) or B1 M1 A1. Longer integration parts run M1 dM1 M1, or M1 M1 B1 A1 M1: you set up the integral, integrate, then substitute limits. Show-that parts end with a final A1, cso, so every step must be visible and correct. An A1ft is occasionally available when you reuse your own value.

where_marks_leak.text: You give a probability or frequency to the wrong number of decimal places or significant figures, or round too early. The final A1 is lost, even though the method marks before it are safe.
You read a bar's height as the frequency instead of multiplying frequency density by class width. The M1 goes, and the A1 after it, along with any dependent mark that uses that frequency.
When integrating by substitution, you keep the original x-limits on the u-integral, or do not substitute back first. The limits mark is lost, and so is the accuracy mark for the value.
When finding a standard deviation for the normal model, you forget to subtract the square of the mean, or divide by the wrong n. The M1 is lost and the A1 for the value goes with it.

write_to_earn: Write frequency density × class width for each bar you use, before you calculate anything.
Write the integral with its limits before integrating, then show the substitution of upper and lower limits.
In a show-that part, write the line just before the printed result, then the result.
Write the variance formula before substituting, and only round on the final line.
For a comment, state which model is closer, quote a figure from each, and give a conclusion in words.
